titre: It Took Demanding a Duel to Abolish It
accroche: In 1817, an acquitted murder suspect throws a gauntlet down in court and demands a duel to the death: English law agrees with him.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 26, 1817, in Birmingham, Mary Ashford, twenty, is walking home from a dance in the early morning. Seven hours later, she is found drowned in a pond. Abraham Thornton, the young man who escorted her, is tried for murder and rape at the Warwick assizes: the trial lasts less than a day, and the jury acquits him in August 1817.

Public opinion cries scandal. William Ashford, the victim's younger brother, then uses a medieval procedure still on the English statute book, the “appeal of murder”: a relative of the victim can restart prosecution after an acquittal, before a different court. Thornton is arrested again. On November 17, 1817, summoned before the Court of King's Bench, he pulls a leather gauntlet from his pocket, throws it at Ashford's feet and declares: “Not guilty; and I am ready to defend the same with my body.” He claims trial by battle, the “wager of battle”: a duel to the death meant to settle the accusation in place of a trial.

## A Right Left on the Books

Nobody had fought a judicial duel before an English court since 1446. But use is not law: no text had ever abolished the wager of battle, it had only fallen into disuse. Ashford's lawyers argue that the evidence against Thornton is strong enough to strip him of this right; on April 16, 1818, the four judges of the court, led by Lord Ellenborough, rule the opposite. Justice Bayley puts it bluntly: whoever invokes this right must be ready to stake his life on it. The evidence is not enough to deprive him of it, and the duel remains his by right. William Ashford, slighter than Thornton, refuses to fight and withdraws his appeal. Thornton is freed.

## What the Refused Duel Changes

Parliament, alarmed that an accused man could legally have demanded a duel to the death in the Georgian era, passes the following year the Appeal of Murder, etc. Act 1819, which abolishes at a stroke the appeal of murder and the wager of battle. The English judicial duel thus did not die with the Middle Ages: it took an accused putting it back on the table of a London court for the law to finally agree to erase it, three centuries after the last duel actually fought. France had settled the matter earlier, in practice: its last authorized judicial duel dates to 1386, the Carrouges v. Le Gris affair. The Holy Roman Empire proscribed it by a text as early as the start of the 16th century, under Maximilian I. Between a practice fallen into disuse and a right formally withdrawn, centuries can pass; it is the latter that counts, since the former can always invoke the law left on the books.

carte.punch: A murder suspect demanded a duel to the death in court: the law agreed with him.
carte.idee: In 1817 in London, Abraham Thornton, acquitted of Mary Ashford's murder, demands a judicial duel to avoid a second trial: the law, never abolished since the Middle Ages, grants it. His opponent backs down, but the scandal pushes Parliament to abolish the procedure in 1819.

quiz.question: Why can Abraham Thornton legally demand a judicial duel in 1817?
choix: Because an 1817 law has just reinstated this procedure for serious charges
Because the wager of battle had never been abolished by statute, only neglected in practice since 1446
Because King George III personally authorized it for this trial
Because the jury that acquitted him recommended this procedure to the judge
quiz.explication: Judicial combat had never been abolished by English law before 1819; it had only fallen into disuse since 1446. No 1817 law reinstates it, the king does not intervene in the procedure, and the jury has no role after an acquittal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What medieval procedure does William Ashford use to restart the prosecution against Thornton after his acquittal?
choix: An appeal on points of law to the House of Lords
The appeal of murder, which lets a relative of the victim restart prosecution
A habeas corpus petition filed by the victim's family
A civil-party complaint before the investigating judge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: William Ashford uses the appeal of murder, a medieval procedure still on the English statute book, which lets a relative of the victim restart prosecution after an acquittal, before a different court.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which law, passed in 1819, abolishes both the appeal of murder and the wager of battle?
choix: The Appeal of Murder, etc. Act 1819
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Parliament passes the Appeal of Murder, etc. Act 1819 the year after the case, abolishing at a stroke the appeal of murder and the wager of battle, alarmed that an accused man could legally have demanded a duel.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year did the last English judicial duel actually fought take place, before Thornton claimed his in 1817?
choix: In 1817, at the Ashford v Thornton trial itself
In 1386, in the French Carrouges v. Le Gris affair
In 1446, in a case pitting a servant against his master
In the early 16th century, under the reign of Maximilian I
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The last English judicial duel actually fought dates to 1446: the Carrouges v. Le Gris affair is French (1386), and the abolition under Maximilian I concerns the Holy Roman Empire, not England.
